article_content: When ‘Toy Story’ was released in 1995, it was revolutionary as the first feature-length computer-animated film. Nearly two decades later, amateur filmmakers Jonason Pauley and Jesse Perrotta reconstructed the movie in live-action as a tribute to the Pixar classic. Jonason Pauley, 19, and Jesse Perrotta, 21, spent nearly two years recreating the iconic movie, and recently uploaded their finished film to YouTube. Two amateur filmmakers recreated 'Toy Story' as a live-action version over two years. A still from the 1995 Pixar version shows Sid torturing Woody, voiced by Tom Hanks. The live-action version depicts Buzz attacking Woody after their initial encounter in Andy's room. Pixar's Buzz uses his laser on Woody in the original film. Mr. Pauley told MailOnline that the two years spent on the project was a labor of love. ‘It was just something fun to do,’ he said, adding that they worked on the movie in their free time. ‘We started filming on Saturdays. Eventually, we had to finish because we were using other people’s time and space.’ He added that ‘Toy Story’ was his favorite childhood film (and still is), having watched it hundreds of times prior to the project. Mr. Pauley said that the actors were mostly friends or acquaintances from church. ‘Andy and Sid are brothers to each other, friends of mine from my old church,’ he said. ‘They fit the part well, and they were always eager to be in my films.’ The full-length film was shot on a consumer camcorder, using green screens, stop-motion animation, and puppetry. Jonason Pauley and Jesse Perrotta spent two years working on their film. After finishing their film, the Arizona-based directors visited Pixar's studios near San Francisco. Woody and Buzz also made the journey. Mr. Pauley was usually behind the camera while Mr. Perrotta operated the puppets, though they sometimes switched roles. Filming a live-action ‘Toy Story’ was challenging. The actors were young volunteers (TJ Bright, Victor Bright, Carla Pauley, Abigale Peters, and Delani Kent), and some scenes required tricky camerawork and post-production. Mr. Pauley said the finale was the most difficult scene, involving the toys chasing Andy in the RV. It was challenging to get the shots with actual dogs and from a moving vehicle. After many hours of shooting and editing, the film was completed. The aliens respond to Buzz in the 'spacecraft' at Pizza Planet. Buzz speaks with the green toy aliens in the Pixar version. Mr. Pauley, a film student at Northern Arizona University, said he and his partner always planned to visit the studios near San Francisco to celebrate. Upon arriving at the Emeryville studios, they were allowed to hand out DVDs of their film. ‘Many Pixar employees were excited to watch it and hear about it,’ he said. The live-action ‘Toy Story’ uses the audio from the original film, featuring Tom Hanks as Woody and Tim Allen as Buzz Lightyear. Mr. Pauley mentioned that the final rescue scene with Woody and Buzz was tricky to film due to the moving shot, real animals, and difficult angles. The original 'Toy Story' cost $30 million to produce and was the first feature-length computer-animated film. While they never received explicit permission to use Pixar’s material, Mr. Pauley said they had tweeted at Pixar executives several times before publishing their work to YouTube and never received a 'no.' ‘They said just do it,’ he said. ‘If they’re okay with it, that’s cool.’ Mr. Pauley said he is happy with the final product, calling it a learning experience. As of Sunday evening, their film had garnered 253,000 views with positive feedback. One viewer wrote: ‘This is so cool on so many levels! Fantastic!’ Pixar’s ‘Toy Story’ had an estimated $30 million budget and grossed over $360 million worldwide. Jesse Perrotta often operated the puppets.

article_content: Sam Burgess has become the first English player to win the Rugby League International Federation's International Player of the Year Award at a ceremony in Australia. Burgess, who played through a fractured eye socket and cheekbone to help South Sydney win the NRL Grand Final, received the prestigious award at the Royal International Convention Centre in Brisbane. The 2014 Four Nations Series is commencing there on Saturday without him. The former Bradford forward will join Bath next week to begin his transition to rugby union. He will not be able to debut until December as he recovers from the injuries sustained in the match against the Canterbury Bulldogs earlier this month. Sam Burgess received the International Player of the Year's Award from former Australian player Wally Lewis. Burgess sustained a significant hit during the NRL Grand Final at ANZ Stadium in Sydney, which his team won. The rugby league star received the award at the Brisbane event, marking him as the first English winner. Burgess recently received another rugby league honor but is transitioning to rugby union with Bath. Past winners of the award (distinct from the Golden Boot) include: 2008 - Billy Slater (Australia) 2009 - Jarryd Hayne (Australia) 2010 - Todd Carney (Australia) 2011 - Billy Slater (Australia) 2012 - Cameron Smith (Australia) 2013 - Sonny Bill Williams (New Zealand) Burgess was selected by a panel of 10 judges from nominees including James Graham, who will captain England against Samoa at Suncorp Stadium on Saturday, Dally M Medal winners Johnathan Thurston and Jarryd Hayne, and Super League Man of Steel Daryl Clark. 'Sam was outstanding for England in the World Cup last year, and his performances for South Sydney throughout the NRL season were exceptional, culminating in his Clive Churchill Medal-winning effort in the Grand Final against Canterbury-Bankstown,' said RLIF chairman Nigel Wood. 'He is a deserving recipient and should be recognized for his accomplishments over the past year, both internationally and in the NRL competition.' Burgess played with a suspected broken cheekbone for South Sydney in the NRL Grand Final. Burgess won the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match before receiving the trophy. article_content: By Beth Stebner PUBLISHED: 09:48 EST, September 8, 2012 | UPDATED: 16:27 EST, September 8, 2012 A Brooklyn-based photographer, who skyrocketed to fame after a well-timed picture of a couple sharing a kiss before being taken to court, may not receive the recognition he deserves. Self-taught street photographer Mo Gelber, who captured Alexis Creque and Russell Murphy outside Manhattan Criminal Court last month, hopes to enter his photograph in a prestigious competition, but there’s a problem. Ms. Creque and Mr. Murphy have not given their consent, which Canon’s ‘Project Imagina10n’ requires. They found love in a hopeless place: Alexis Creque, 28, kisses her boyfriend, Russell Murphy, in this perfectly timed snapshot after their arrest. Race against the clock: Street photographer Mo Gelber's photo was at risk of disqualification because he needed consent forms. Mr. Gelber told MailOnline that he had until 5 p.m. to obtain the couple’s consent. As the deadline passed, his photograph was no longer eligible. 'I have not heard back from Alexis, and she deactivated her Facebook page. Maybe she got spooked,' he said earlier today. The young woman said her boyfriend was expected to be released from jail sometime Saturday and had previously indicated that she would help only after his release. Adding to the complications, a disparaging note was slipped under her apartment door. According to the New York Post, the note read: ‘F*** Off.’ He told MailOnline after the 5 p.m. deadline: 'Because of some legal issues, one of the four parties was not comfortable with some of the terms in the release.' But he is not bitter. ‘I don’t have any hard feelings toward anybody,' he said. 'The fact that a judge in the competition considers my photo a candidate for the finals means a lot to me. Being considered a finalist, I already consider myself a winner.’ Mr. Gelber is doing all he can to ensure the couple receives credit and has promised to share any money he makes from the viral ‘Last Kiss’ photo with them. He quipped: ‘I’ll just tell him don’t use (the money) to buy spray paint.’ Canon’s rules state that if the photo depicts any person other than the photographer, their written consent must be obtained, which also applies to the two NYPD officers in the frame. One of the police officers has signed a release, but the other is on vacation. Even though the deadline passed without the consent forms submitted to Canon, Mr. Gelber said his mission has been accomplished. 'My ultimate goal of entering the contest was to gain recognition as a photojournalist,' he said, noting that the image has spread rapidly online. 'I’ll go with the flow,' he said, adding: 'I’m being realistic, so it’s fine either way. If I put all my cards on the table, I might be setting myself up for disappointment.' Who's that girl? Alexis Creque, pictured, contacted the photographer to reveal she was the woman in the picture. She said she was arrested in Manhattan on August 16 while watching her boyfriend allegedly spray graffiti outside an exclusive bar. Mr. Gelber, 42, identified the couple through social media. Ms. Creque contacted Mr. Gelber through Facebook to admit she was the blonde-haired woman kissing her handcuffed boyfriend, identified in a police report as 26-year-old Russell Murphy, while being taken to Manhattan Criminal Court last month. Mr. Gelber specializes in street photography, capturing candid emotions. 'One of my specialties is candid street photos that capture the rolling emotions of people. Part of it is predicting what people do and anticipating it,' he said. He happened to be there hoping to photograph the accused Manhattan Madam, Anna Gristina. He was standing next to dozens of other photographers but happened to be looking in the right direction. The criminal report reveals Creque, who lives three blocks from where the alleged crime occurred, was charged with criminal mischief and making graffiti. Her boyfriend stands accused of criminal mischief, making graffiti, resisting arrest, and possession of graffiti instruments. Whether they agree to sign or not, he has printed copies of the picture for them, which Ms. Creque admired. In her message, 'she said she loved it,' he told MailOnline. 'Maybe they are proud of what they did. Maybe they think they did something artistic. The photograph captures that moment.' When tracing the couple, he posted on Facebook on August 17: 'Help!!! Does anyone know who this couple is? It is very important. I took this photo outside Manhattan criminal court on Thursday, August 16th.' 'I entered this photo in a major contest which I am about to win and need them to sign a release form. When this photo wins the contest, they will be in a very big movie with famous actors and directors.' The competition involves famous faces who will try their hand at film-making for the first time. Further details will be announced during the results next week, Mr. Gelber said. The image is reminiscent of another moment captured in chaos: Scott Jones and Alex Thomas kissing amid the Vancouver Stanley Cup riots in June 2011. Getty Images photographer Richard Lam captured the two kissing on the ground, surrounded by riot police and illuminated by flames. In the attempt to identify Mr. Jones, he was dubbed 'Riot Romeo.' Calm in the midst of chaos: Scott Jones embraced his girlfriend Alexandra Thomas during the riots in Vancouver in June 2011, after the Canucks lost the Stanley Cup. The photograph garnered global attention. Riot Romeo: The photograph earned Mr. Jones the nickname 'Riot Romeo'; the images were captured by Getty Images photographer Rich Lam.

article_content: I was surprised and honestly saddened to hear about Melanie Griffith and Antonio Banderas' divorce. I had always considered them an exciting couple. They were both passionate individuals who succeeded in a challenging industry, each with a slightly turbulent past. Griffith had been married three times before Banderas, twice to Don Johnson. Banderas had one previous marriage and certainly embodied the 'Latin lover' archetype. Yet, they seemed deeply in love and remarkably committed to each other for many years. I realize that Hollywood marriages face unique pressures that threaten their stability. However, regardless of their fame, they are still real people who enter marriage hoping for a lifelong commitment. Because of their celebrity, we follow their lives in tabloids and lifestyle magazines, becoming, in a way, invested in their well-being. Upon reading the news of their separation, I realized I had wanted them to stay together indefinitely, hoping their private lives would mirror the 'happily ever after' endings of their films. I believed their connection was deep and strong enough to endure. Perhaps my sadness stemmed from recognizing my own unrealistic expectations. While Hollywood marriages encounter specific challenges that diminish their chances of lasting, the reality is that even for average couples, reaching 18 or 20 years together provides no guarantee of continued success. Marriages today can dissolve at any point. The famously enduring marriage of Paul Newman and Joanne Woodward appears more exceptional than typical. Indeed, Newman and Woodward belonged to a generation with different values, a mold that seems to be broken now. Even marriages lasting decades offer no assurance of permanence. Consider Robert Redford and Lola Van Wagenen (27 years) or Jerry Lewis and Patti Palmer (36 years). Statistics show that divorce rates have seen a significant increase among individuals over 50 [Source: Pew Research Center or similar reputable source]. Thus, if you thought age offered protection to your relationship, reconsider. Lifetime marriage is becoming increasingly uncertain, especially for Baby Boomers. Perhaps 'til death do us part' is less likely for Hollywood stars, whose careers strain their relationships and whose divorces are not generally complicated by financial constraints. However, no marriage is invulnerable to this apparent epidemic of marital breakdown. So, we must do what we can to improve our odds of staying together. To me, this means intentionally nurturing our relationship every day, year, and decade we share. We should aim high, enjoy each other's company, work diligently to be both lovers and friends, and consistently address issues that arise. If it ends, it ends, but it shouldn't end without every effort to keep it alive. Therefore, let's be realistic; we can't predict the future. I considered this as I looked at a photo of Melanie Griffith and noticed a large tattoo on her arm that read 'Antonio.' That’s a warning sign, I thought. If you desire a name tattooed on your body, choose your mother's or your first pet's name. Otherwise, learn from Melanie, Antonio, and countless others: Even long marriages face an uncertain future. I'm not suggesting planning an exit strategy while trying to build a strong relationship, but I am suggesting taking care and having a Plan B.

article_content: Having a sick day turned out to be incredibly fortunate for teenager Evan Hall, who shared a 'man hug' with Bruce Springsteen in front of 38,000 fans at the Ricoh stadium in Coventry. The 19-year-old has become an internet sensation after being plucked from the crowd to hug and dance with The Boss on stage. Springsteen noticed Evan's homemade sign asking 'Can I have man hug?' as he performed 'Hungry Heart,' one of his most popular songs. Bruce Springsteen spotted Evan Hall's homemade sign requesting a 'man hug' during the concert at the Ricoh stadium in Coventry. The 19-year-old has become an internet star after being chosen from the audience to hug and dance with Springsteen on stage in front of 38,000 fans. He invited Evan onto the stage, and the warmth of the veteran rocker's embrace, combined with Evan's joy and the audience's enthusiastic response, made it a concert highlight. Evan revealed that he had only made the sign the day before because he was home sick and had some free time. 'I noticed at Bruce's previous concerts that people held up signs for song requests, but recently they had become more creative, so I decided to do the same.' The singer was performing his hit song 'Hungry Heart' when he made Evan's wish come true last Thursday. He says he is still thrilled after what he calls 'the best moment of my life'. 'It's beyond anything I have ever experienced. I was hyperventilating; it was just so lovely, and the audience's reaction was fantastic.' 'When I got on stage, I said to Bruce, 'Thank you, so, so much,' and he was laughing. He told me to look at the amazing audience and said, 'This is what I see every day.' It was just amazing.' Evan had driven to the Ricoh with his father, Dale – a huge Springsteen fan who used to sing his baby son to sleep with Springsteen’s hits – from their home in Edwinstowe near Mansfield in Nottinghamshire. They spent the night in a Coventry car park before queuing early to ensure they were at the front of the stage. 'My dad thinks it's brilliant, but when I came off stage, he said, 'I've been waiting 30 years for that, and it happened to you.'' Evan is familiar with Coventry, although it was his first visit to the Ricoh. Evan had driven down to the Ricoh with his father Dale – a huge Springsteen fan who used to sing his baby son to sleep with the Boss's hits – from their home at Edwinstowe near Mansfield in Nottinghamshire. 'I already liked Coventry. I work there often in care homes as a trainee fire and security alarms engineer.' 'I've passed the Ricoh many times on my way, but I never thought it would be the place where I'd have the greatest moment of my life.' He's been to seven Springsteen concerts, but only one with his girlfriend, Zoe, who isn't a big fan. Evan said, 'She was getting a bit annoyed with people contacting me at first. I've had calls from all over the world from fans wanting to talk about the concert.' 'But when she saw the videos and saw how much joy it's given to people, she found it very touching.' Evan, who shares his first name with Springsteen's eldest son, said memories of 'Hungry Heart' and Coventry will stay with him forever. He has even earned a mention in the official Wrecking Ball tour notes, which say: 'A fan caught Bruce’s attention with a sign asking, 'Bruce, can I have a man hug?' Yes, you can… he was rewarded with not one but four hugs, and a little dance too. Bruce was working hard to keep his fans happy.'

Si è persino guadagnato una menzione nelle note ufficiali del tour di Wrecking Ball, che recitano: 'Un fan ha attirato l'attenzione di Bruce con un cartello che chiedeva: 'Bruce, posso avere un abbraccio da uomo?' article_content: After passengers subdued a pilot behaving erratically on JetBlue Flight 191, questions arise: Will JetBlue discontinue using this flight number? A Wall Street Journal blogger noted that flight number 191 has been associated with multiple disasters. In 1985, Delta Air Lines Flight 191 crashed near Dallas-Fort Worth, resulting in 137 fatalities. The airline then retired the flight number. Prior to that, American Airlines retired flight number 191 following a 1979 crash shortly after takeoff from Chicago's O'Hare airport. That incident killed 271 passengers and crew, plus two on the ground. At the time, it was the deadliest aviation disaster in U.S. history until 9/11, leading to a temporary grounding of all DC-10 aircraft to address technical issues. Despite the string of misfortunes connected to the number 191 and the aviation industry's superstitious tendencies, the Huffington Post reports that JetBlue currently intends to keep using the flight number.

Precedentemente, American Airlines aveva ritirato il numero di volo 191 a seguito di un incidente nel 1979, poco dopo il decollo dall'aeroporto di O'Hare a Chicago. In quell'incidente persero la vita 271 passeggeri e membri dell'equipaggio, oltre a due persone a terra. article_content: A robot that can print new 'body' parts for itself and adapt to different environments has been created. In a video, the machine is shown struggling, but succeeding, to crawl along the ground after having one of its four limbs removed. This could foreshadow future robots capable of learning how to overcome difficult conditions on other planets, such as Mars. Scientists at the University of Oslo have created robots that can learn to adapt. These multi-limbed machines can overcome environmental challenges. In a video, a robot with a limb removed learns how to walk (shown). The robots were created by a team of scientists from the University of Oslo. To make them, a 3D printer is fed a list of parameters, including desired speed, size, and efficiency. A simulator then pits several different creations in 'fights to the death' before the winning robot is sent to the 3D printer for production. The robot was then 'taught' that it was missing a limb and instructed to try and walk across the floor. In the video, it can be seen how the robot adapts to its situation and still manages to 'walk' or crawl across the floor. The 3D printers used by the university cost up to £280,000 ($430,000) and are capable of extremely high precision. The robots were created by a team of scientists from the University of Oslo. To make them, a 3D printer is fed a list of parameters including desired speed, size, and efficiency. A simulator then pits several different creations with different limbs and features in 'fights to the death' before selecting a winner. Robots of the future won't just be smart; they could also have ninja-like reflexes. Researchers in the US are studying how cats and athletes rotate their bodies mid-air and hope to recreate that movement in droids. The aim is to reduce the impact on falling robots, especially those that may one day be used for search-and-rescue missions in hazardous conditions. Professor Karen Liu at Georgia Tech University has been simulating the physics of everything from falling cats to the mid-air orientation of divers and astronauts. The study involved using a small robot consisting of a main body and two symmetric legs with paddles. According to IEEE Spectrum, the potential benefits of such a robot are numerous. For example, a Mars rover equipped with a 3D printer could autonomously extract itself from difficult situations. 'In the future, robots must be able to solve tasks in deep mines, on distant planets, in radioactive disaster areas, in hazardous landslip areas, and on the seabed beneath the Antarctic,' said Professor Kyrre Glette, from the Robotics and Intelligent Systems research group. 'These environments are so extreme that no human being can cope. Everything needs to be automatically controlled.' 'Imagine that the robot is entering the wreckage of a nuclear power plant. It finds a staircase that no one has thought of.' 'The robot takes a picture. The picture is analyzed. The arms of one of the robots are fitted with a printer.' 'This produces a new robot, or a new part for the existing robot, which enables it to negotiate the stairs.' The research team (shown with some of the robots) say that the technique of autonomously creating parts could be used by future robots on other planets in the solar system.

article_content: Ramon Rojas, a world-renowned base jumper known as 'The Birdman,' has died while practicing his sport. The Chilean sportsman passed away during a competition in Lauterbrunnen, Switzerland, on Saturday, according to reports. The 35-year-old athlete set records last month with a 4,100m jump from El Plomo mountain in the Andes, near Santiago, Chile. Tributes are being offered to the celebrated base jumper, also known as Chapa. A Facebook page, 'Ramon Rojas Memorial to Celebrate his Awesome Life,' has been created for friends to share heartfelt messages. Group founder Monica Vasquez Burrier wrote, 'I felt honored by your friendship. You were pure energy of joy, kindness, and the best values in a man. Fly free forever, my friend; you will be deeply missed by many people you touched with your light.’ Another tribute stated, 'You left for eternity doing what you loved most. Now you can take the great flights of the soul, where everything is ethereal and beautiful.’ Jamie Nicholl, along with others, changed his profile picture to a black square as a sign of respect, writing, ‘RIP big fella, fly free.’ Base jumping involves participants jumping from fixed objects and using a parachute to slow their descent. The circumstances surrounding the accident remain unclear. However, The Mirror reports that Chilean newspaper La Tercera suggests preliminary investigations indicate strong winds may have caused him to lose control. The website Base Jump Chile stated that Ramon Rojas was born in Cachapoal Valley, Chile, adding, 'At an early age, he fell in love with the mountains, a relationship that defined his philosophy of life: enjoy every minute surrounded by nature.'

article_content: The death of Shani Louk, a 23-year-old German-Israeli woman whose semi-naked body was paraded through the streets of Gaza by Hamas militants, has been confirmed. "We are devastated to share that the death of 23-year-old German-Israeli Shani Louk was confirmed," Israel's foreign ministry said on X (formerly Twitter). "Shani, who was kidnapped from a music festival and tortured before being paraded around Gaza by Hamas terrorists, experienced unfathomable horrors. Our hearts are broken. May her memory be a blessing." Louk's mother, Ricarda Louk, told German broadcaster RTL/ntv that Israeli officials identified a skull fragment as her daughter's based on DNA evidence. Louk had been attending a music festival near Kibbutz Re'im when Hamas militants stormed the area on October 7, killing more than 260 people. In total, more than 1,400 people were killed and over 200 were kidnapped in the Hamas attacks on Israel that day, which targeted the festival, towns, and military bases. In the footage, the woman appeared to be stripped to her underwear, and her legs were bent at unnatural angles while one militant grabbed her hair. People were also seen spitting on her body. Her face wasn't visible, but her dreadlocks and tattoos helped her family identify her as Louk, The Washington Post reported. Days after the attack, her mother, Ricarda Louk, told Bild that her daughter had called her from the festival, saying she was looking for ways to flee with her boyfriend and others. She told her daughter to seek refuge at a local shelter but then heard gunfire on the other end of the phone, she told the outlet. Ricarda told Bild that Palestinian sources had told her that her daughter was alive in a Hamas hospital but had suffered a 'severe head injury.' "We now have reasons to believe that Shani is alive but has had a severe head injury and is in critical condition. Every minute is critical," Ricarda told Bild at the time. However, speaking to German broadcaster RTL/ntv on Monday, Ricarda said she now believes her daughter had been dead since October 7. "Unfortunately, we received news yesterday that my daughter is no longer alive," she said. In the RTL interview, Ricarda said a skull fragment indicated she had likely been killed on October 7 by a bullet to the head. It is unclear where the fragment of her skull was found. IDF spokesman Rear Adm. Daniel Hagari told The Times of Israel on Sunday that 239 people had now been confirmed kidnapped in the October 7 attacks. The number does not include the four hostages released by Hamas. Israeli forces have launched waves of airstrikes in Gaza following the October 7 attacks, which Palestinian authorities say have killed more than 8,000 people. With the Israeli military intensifying its operations in Gaza, the families of Israeli hostages on Saturday expressed concern for their safety and urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to secure their release, CNN reported.

Il portavoce dell'IDF, il contrammiraglio Daniel Hagari, ha dichiarato al Times of Israel domenica che 239 persone sono state confermate rapite negli attacchi del 7 ottobre. Il numero non include i quattro ostaggi rilasciati da Hamas. Le forze israeliane hanno lanciato ondate di attacchi aerei su Gaza in seguito agli attacchi del 7 ottobre, che, secondo le autorità palestinesi, hanno causato la morte di oltre 8.000 persone. Con l'esercito israeliano che intensifica le operazioni a Gaza, sabato le famiglie degli ostaggi israeliani hanno espresso preoccupazione per la loro sicurezza e hanno esortato il Primo Ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu a garantire il loro rilascio, come riportato dalla CNN.

article_content: According to a study released today, homeowners in Corby, located in the East Midlands, face the highest risk of home repossession. The study examined repossession hotspots across the country. The Northamptonshire town of Corby has the largest proportion of homeowners who have received a possession order for their homes in the past year, the research indicates. Following Corby, areas with high repossession rates include Barking and Dagenham and Newham in London, Knowsley in Merseyside, and Thurrock in Essex. A report accompanying the figures cautioned that homeowners nationwide should prepare for potentially higher mortgage repayments when interest rates are expected to increase later in the year. A possession order signifies an advanced stage in the repossession process, indicating that a homeowner is at significant risk of losing their home. The study revealed that Corby's rate of possession orders is nine times higher than that of West Dorset, which had the lowest rate. The housing and homelessness charity Shelter conducted the study, identifying 65 out of 324 local authorities as repossession hotspots. Many of these are areas with high unemployment. Significant concentrations of repossession hotspots were identified in areas around Tyneside, Yorkshire, Leeds, Liverpool, The Wash, Southeast London, and the coastal towns of Kent and Essex. The average unemployment rate in local authorities with the highest repossession rates was 9.6 percent, compared to 5.3 percent in those with the lowest rates. The study by Shelter also found that unemployment in the most at-risk areas has risen by an average of 3.3 percent over the past three years, compared to a 1.4 percent increase in the areas with the lowest risk. The research highlighted clusters of local authorities at highest risk, including Tyneside, the Kent coastal towns (Thurrock, Medway, Swale), and The Wash (South Holland, Fenland, Peterborough). Additionally, the study identified a 'ribbon' of repossessions across northern England, extending from the Mersey in the west to the Humber estuary in the east. The findings were based on an analysis of the latest Ministry of Justice figures, which detailed the rates of claims leading to possession orders per 1,000 households for each local authority. These figures were published in May 2011. Campbell Robb, chief executive of Shelter, stated: 'This research paints a concerning picture of repossession hotspots across the country, where homeowners are at imminent risk of losing their homes.' 'We are acutely aware that the combined impact of high inflation, rising living costs, and stagnant wages is significantly affecting people.' 'A single event, such as job loss, can push individuals into a cycle of debt, repossession, and ultimately homelessness.'

article_content: One of the key demands stemming from the national wave of demonstrations protesting recent police killings of unarmed black men is for law enforcement agencies to expand the practice of equipping officers with dashboard cameras, body cameras, and other recording devices. The idea is that visual recordings of controversial encounters will make it easier to uncover the truth in situations like the shooting of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, or the death of Eric Garner in New York. Activists across the country have criticized the lack of a grand jury indictment in either case. However, a strong word of caution is warranted for those who believe the widespread use of cameras will reduce or eliminate instances of police brutality or unjustified killings. The available evidence does not clearly indicate that cameras will have the promised beneficial effects. The public's desire to see what happened is understandable. 'We won't have to play this game of witnesses' memories and secret grand juries' if cameras are more widely used, says Benjamin Crump, the Brown family attorney, who is advocating for what he calls the Michael Brown law. 'It'll just be transparent, and we can see it for ourselves. We can hold people accountable when they interact with citizens.' This idea is gaining traction. President Obama announced a $263 million package to help local police departments buy and use 50,000 cameras, and the New York Police Department, the nation's largest, launched a pilot program. But Justin Ready and Jacob Young, criminology professors at Arizona State University, argue that cameras often have unintended negative consequences. 'In our field research on body cameras, there have been many times when cameras made matters worse for the officer,' the professors write. 'For example, in one situation, an officer was trying to comfort a teenage girl who lived in an abusive home, but he found it difficult to show compassion and respect for her privacy with the camera rolling. ...The device can be a physical reminder to crime victims that they are on camera at times when they are most vulnerable and in need of privacy.' Since statistics show that fewer than 20% of police calls involve felony crimes and only 1% of calls result in the use of physical force, the majority of recordings will capture vulnerable victims rather than document instances of police using force. There's also the question of whether witnesses will be less willing to share information with officers if they suspect the conversation is being recorded. Another problem is whether officers will simply turn off cameras at crucial moments. In early 2014, in New Orleans, a police officer shot Armand Bennett in the forehead during a traffic stop, then failed to report the incident (for which the city's police chief later apologized). The press discovered that the officer who shot Bennett had a body camera, but it was switched off. In San Diego, two controversial shootings were captured on police body-cam videos this year, but police refused media requests to make the footage public, undermining the idea that video records can help the public understand what happens in controversial cases. Even when camera footage is available, Ready and Young say, 'it is possible that on-officer video creates a polarizing effect on some controversies because people with strong convictions about what has transpired during a police shooting may use the 'facts' that they see in the video footage to support their expectations about what occurred in the blind spots.' Washington Post blogger Radley Balko points out that simply having cameras isn't enough: 'In addition to making these videos public record, accessible through public records requests, we also need to ensure that police agencies implement rules requiring officers to actually use the cameras, enforce those rules by disciplining officers when they don't, and ensure that the officers, the agencies that employ them, and prosecutors all take care to preserve footage, even if the footage reflects poorly on officers.' An additional problem is that evidence suggests the presence of cameras doesn't necessarily make police officers more courteous or careful. A well-publicized study of police in Rialto, California, found that using cameras led to a 60% drop in the use of force and an 88% decline in citizen complaints in a single year. However, that experience is not universal. Dashboard cameras had been in use in Seattle for years, but in 2011 a federal Justice Department investigation still concluded that the department 'engages in a pattern or practice of using unnecessary or excessive force.' According to Ready and Young, 'police are actually more proactive when wearing cameras,' in part because they can record circumstances that will support their reasons for taking action. As the nation prepares for the next 50,000 body-cams to hit the street, we'll face the same underlying question: Are the cops keeping us safe while also respecting everyone's civil liberties and constitutional rights? That's a question no amount of technology can answer.
translated_content: Una delle principali richieste derivanti dall'ondata nazionale di manifestazioni contro le recenti uccisioni di uomini neri disarmati da parte della polizia è che le forze dell'ordine estendano l'uso di telecamere da cruscotto, telecamere indossabili e altri dispositivi di registrazione per gli agenti. L'idea è che le registrazioni visive di incontri controversi renderanno più facile scoprire la verità in situazioni come la sparatoria di Michael Brown a Ferguson, nel Missouri, o la morte di Eric Garner a New York. Gli attivisti di tutto il paese hanno criticato la mancanza di un incriminazione da parte del grand jury in entrambi i casi. Tuttavia, è doveroso mettere in guardia coloro che credono che l'uso diffuso di telecamere ridurrà o eliminerà i casi di brutalità della polizia o di uccisioni ingiustificate. Le prove disponibili non indicano chiaramente che le telecamere avranno gli effetti benefici promessi. Il desiderio del pubblico di vedere cosa è successo è comprensibile. 'Non dovremo più giocare a questo gioco dei ricordi dei testimoni e dei grand jury segreti' se le telecamere saranno più ampiamente utilizzate, afferma Benjamin Crump, l'avvocato della famiglia Brown, che sta sostenendo quella che chiama la legge Michael Brown. 'Sarà tutto trasparente e potremo vederlo da soli. Possiamo ritenere le persone responsabili quando interagiscono con i cittadini.' Questa idea sta guadagnando terreno. Il presidente Obama ha annunciato un pacchetto da 263 milioni di dollari per aiutare i dipartimenti di polizia locali ad acquistare e utilizzare 50.000 telecamere, e il dipartimento di polizia di New York, il più grande della nazione, ha lanciato un programma pilota. Ma Justin Ready e Jacob Young, professori di criminologia all'Arizona State University, sostengono che le telecamere hanno spesso conseguenze negative non intenzionali. 'Nella nostra ricerca sul campo sulle telecamere indossabili, ci sono state molte volte in cui le telecamere hanno peggiorato le cose per l'agente', scrivono i professori. 'Ad esempio, in una situazione, un agente stava cercando di confortare una ragazza adolescente che viveva in una casa violenta, ma ha avuto difficoltà a mostrare compassione e rispetto per la sua privacy con la telecamera accesa. ...Il dispositivo può essere un promemoria fisico per le vittime di crimini che sono riprese dalla telecamera in momenti in cui sono più vulnerabili e bisognose di privacy.' Poiché le statistiche mostrano che meno del 20% delle chiamate alla polizia riguarda crimini gravi e solo l'1% delle chiamate si traduce nell'uso della forza fisica, la maggior parte delle registrazioni catturerà vittime vulnerabili piuttosto che documentare casi di uso della forza da parte della polizia. C'è anche la questione se i testimoni saranno meno disposti a condividere informazioni con gli agenti se sospettano che la conversazione venga registrata. Un altro problema è se gli agenti spegneranno semplicemente le telecamere nei momenti cruciali. All'inizio del 2014, a New Orleans, un agente di polizia ha sparato ad Armand Bennett alla fronte durante un controllo del traffico, quindi non ha denunciato l'incidente (per il quale il capo della polizia della città si è successivamente scusato). La stampa ha scoperto che l'agente che ha sparato a Bennett aveva una telecamera indossabile, ma era spenta. A San Diego, due sparatorie controverse sono state riprese dai video delle telecamere indossabili della polizia quest'anno, ma la polizia ha rifiutato le richieste dei media di rendere pubblico il filmato, minando l'idea che le registrazioni video possano aiutare il pubblico a capire cosa succede in casi controversi. Anche quando il filmato della telecamera è disponibile, Ready e Young affermano: 'è possibile che il video sull'agente crei un effetto polarizzante su alcune controversie, perché le persone con forti convinzioni su ciò che è accaduto durante una sparatoria della polizia possono usare i 'fatti' che vedono nel filmato video per supportare le loro aspettative su ciò che è accaduto negli angoli ciechi.' Il blogger del Washington Post Radley Balko sottolinea che la semplice presenza di telecamere non è sufficiente: 'Oltre a rendere pubblici questi video, accessibili tramite richieste di documenti pubblici, dobbiamo anche assicurarci che le agenzie di polizia implementino regole che richiedano agli agenti di utilizzare effettivamente le telecamere, applichino tali regole disciplinando gli agenti quando non lo fanno e si assicurino che gli agenti, le agenzie che li impiegano e i pubblici ministeri si prendano tutti cura di conservare il filmato, anche se il filmato si riflette negativamente sugli agenti.' Un ulteriore problema è che le prove suggeriscono che la presenza di telecamere non rende necessariamente gli agenti di polizia più cortesi o attenti. Uno studio ben pubblicizzato sulla polizia di Rialto, in California, ha scoperto che l'uso di telecamere ha portato a un calo del 60% nell'uso della forza e a un calo dell'88% nelle denunce dei cittadini in un solo anno. Tuttavia, questa esperienza non è universale. Le telecamere da cruscotto erano in uso a Seattle da anni, ma nel 2011 un'indagine federale del Dipartimento di Giustizia ha comunque concluso che il dipartimento 'si impegna in un modello o pratica di uso di forza non necessaria o eccessiva.' Secondo Ready e Young, 'la polizia è in realtà più proattiva quando indossa telecamere', in parte perché possono registrare circostanze che supporteranno le loro ragioni per intraprendere azioni. Mentre la nazione si prepara ai prossimi 50.000 body-cam che arriveranno nelle strade, affronteremo la stessa domanda di fondo: i poliziotti ci tengono al sicuro e rispettano anche le libertà civili e i diritti costituzionali di tutti? Questa è una domanda a cui nessuna quantità di tecnologia può rispondere.

article_content: An NHS hospital trust losing £1 million a week has been placed into administration to prevent its collapse, the Department of Health announced today. Health Secretary Andrew Lansley has appointed a trust special administrator to attempt to turn around the struggling South London Healthcare NHS Trust. The trust is in danger of following the South London Healthcare NHS Trust, which operates three hospitals, including Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Woolwich (pictured), and was put under the charge of a special administrator due to being on the brink of bankruptcy. Mr. Lansley stated: 'I have decided it is in the best interests of the health service and, particularly, of the patients the Trust serves.' The Trust has been placed on an 'unsustainable providers regime,' and the government has appointed Matthew Kershaw to put it back on a 'viable footing.' Mr. Kershaw is currently the national director for provider delivery at the Department of Health. He will assume control of the Trust's board on Monday, July 16, and provide recommendations to Mr. Lansley at the beginning of next year. The chairs and directors have been informed of their suspension from board duties. This marks the first time in NHS history that a trust has been compelled to cede its administration powers to the Department of Health after failing to meet prescribed standards. Matthew Kershaw is the special administrator tasked with resolving the Trust's issues. The Trust was established in 2009 following the merger of three hospitals: the Princess Royal Hospital in Orpington, Queen Mary's Hospital in Sidcup, and Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Woolwich. However, it has accumulated £150 million in debt over the past three years, largely due to crippling Private Finance Initiative deals agreed upon by the previous Labour government. The two PFI deals are now costing £61 million annually in interest. Last year's deficit, covered by funds from elsewhere in the NHS budget, could have funded 1,200 nurses or 200 hip replacements per week. The Health Secretary intervened after draft financial plans indicated the trust would face a deficit of between £30 million and £75 million per year for the next five years, despite efforts to address the situation. Today he said: 'Previous efforts have not succeeded in placing the South London Healthcare Trust on a sustainable path.' 'This will be a significant challenge, and my primary objective for all NHS Trusts is to ensure they deliver high-quality services to patients that are clinically and financially sustainable in the long term.' 'The purpose of the trust special administrator is to ensure services are of high quality and to secure a lasting clinical and financial solution.' Health Secretary Andrew Lansley stated the decision was in the interest of patients. 'Although there have been some improvements in mortality rates, maternity services, and infection control, and some early indications of improvements in waiting times, they are insufficient.' It will be impossible for South London to build upon these improvements while addressing such a substantial deficit. 'Matthew, working with clinicians, all other staff, commissioners, patients, the public, and other stakeholders, must now drive the changes and shape a sustainable solution for South London Healthcare NHS Trust and the local health economy.' 'I am confident that with the regime I am enacting today in place, and working extensively with clinicians, health service leaders, patients, and local people, Matthew will have the tools and framework to find a long-term satisfactory solution for the people of south east London.' Mr. Kershaw will initially publish a report on October 29 after examining the Trust's long-standing difficulties. He will then initiate a 30-day consultation with staff, patients, and the public on a draft report. A final report will be submitted to Mr. Lansley on January 8, 2013. Mr. Kershaw commented: 'My priority is to collaborate with staff, patients, the public, and all those involved in healthcare services in the south east London area to maintain high-quality, effective services during the running of the Unsustainable Provider Regime.' 'This means developing recommendations that ensure that people in south east London can access high-quality, safe, and financially sustainable NHS services for the long-term.' 'Together, we will need to think differently, be bold, and accept that change needs to occur. The status quo is not sustainable.' A spokesperson for the Royal College of Nursing stated: 'This announcement is an unprecedented step by the Secretary of State and moves the NHS into uncharted waters.' 'It presents a worrying state of affairs for both patients and staff at the Trust, who will undoubtedly be concerned by today’s decision.' 'We know that the Trust has been in financial difficulties for some time. However, despite this, frontline staff have continued to do their best for patients, providing a high level of care.'

'Matthew, lavorando con medici, tutto il personale, i commissari, i pazienti, il pubblico e le altre parti interessate, deve ora guidare i cambiamenti e dare forma a una soluzione sostenibile per il South London Healthcare NHS Trust e l'economia sanitaria locale'. 'Sono fiducioso che, con il regime che sto mettendo in atto oggi e lavorando ampiamente con medici, leader del servizio sanitario, pazienti e cittadini, Matthew avrà gli strumenti e le risorse per trovare una soluzione soddisfacente a lungo termine per la popolazione del sud-est di Londra'. Il signor Kershaw pubblicherà inizialmente una relazione il 29 ottobre, dopo aver esaminato le difficoltà di vecchia data del Trust. Avvierà quindi una consultazione di 30 giorni con il personale, i pazienti e il pubblico su una bozza di relazione. Una relazione finale sarà inviata al signor Lansley l'8 gennaio 2013. Il signor Kershaw ha commentato: 'La mia priorità è collaborare con il personale, i pazienti, il pubblico e tutti coloro che sono coinvolti nei servizi sanitari nell'area sud-est di Londra per mantenere servizi efficienti e di alta qualità, durante l'attuazione del regime di fornitori insostenibile'. 'Ciò significa sviluppare raccomandazioni che garantiscano ai cittadini del sud-est di Londra l'accesso a servizi NHS sicuri, di alta qualità e finanziariamente sostenibili a lungo termine'. 'Insieme, dovremo pensare in modo diverso, essere audaci e accettare che il cambiamento è necessario. Lo status quo non è sostenibile'. Un portavoce del Royal College of Nursing ha dichiarato: 'Questo annuncio rappresenta un passo senza precedenti da parte del Segretario di Stato e sposta il NHS in acque inesplorate'. 'Presenta una situazione preoccupante sia per i pazienti che per il personale del Trust, che saranno senza dubbio preoccupati dalla decisione odierna'. 'Sappiamo che il Trust è in difficoltà finanziarie da tempo. Tuttavia, nonostante ciò, il personale in prima linea ha continuato a fare del proprio meglio per i pazienti, fornendo un elevato livello di assistenza'.

article_content: The Supreme Court's final days of June, often called 'flood season,' involve a concentrated effort to complete work before summer recess. This term is especially significant, with rulings expected on two major issues that could profoundly impact lives and legal precedents. On Monday, the court addressed race-conscious school admissions at the University of Texas but referred the case back to lower courts, avoiding a broad decision on whether these policies violate the equal protection rights of some white applicants. Key issues awaiting decisions include:   -- Same-sex marriage: Appeals testing the constitutional right of gay and lesbian couples to marry.   -- Voting rights: The future of the Voting Rights Act and federal oversight of elections in states with a history of discrimination. According to Thomas Goldstein, a prominent Washington attorney, the court's decisions will affect all Americans. He anticipates the court may not fully uphold the Voting Rights Act's enforcement provisions and might seek a middle ground on same-sex marriage, avoiding a definitive ruling for or against it. The court's schedule for releasing these sensitive opinions is not fixed, but it aims to conclude its work by Thursday or early July. Justices have already voted on pending cases after oral arguments. Individual justices are drafting opinions, dissents, and concurrences in secrecy. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg noted the court's tradition of discretion, stating, 'At the Supreme Court, those who know, don't talk. And those who talk, don't know.' The court aims to finalize draft opinions by June 1, with dissents and concurrences due by June 15. Final votes can change. Justices and law clerks are working intensely to finalize opinions, ensuring factual accuracy and legal soundness. The decisions will shape the justices' legacies. While outcomes may be disputed, the constitutional reasoning must be sound. Predicting outcomes is a common practice in Washington, but not consistently accurate. The same-sex marriage cases have drawn significant attention, with activists rallying during March arguments. Key issues include:   -- Federal benefits: The Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) defines marriage federally as between one man and one woman, impacting federal benefits for same-sex couples. Edie Windsor faced significant estate taxes after her spouse's death due to DOMA.   -- State referendums: The court is considering whether a state can revoke same-sex marriage rights after granting them, as happened in California with Proposition 8. The court's decision will place it at the center of national attention, similar to its involvement in the Affordable Care Act ruling. Nine states and the District of Columbia currently allow same-sex marriage. Delaware, Rhode Island, and Minnesota recently passed laws to that effect. Approximately 120,000 legally married same-sex couples reside in the U.S. Differing views exist on whether the court should issue a broad ruling on equal protection. Some suggest elected officials should lead on same-sex marriage, noting voter approval in several states. California is the only state to have both allowed and revoked same-sex marriage. Goldstein believes the court is unlikely to mandate same-sex marriage recognition nationwide, preferring incremental steps. The justices are aware of evolving social norms and may avoid contradicting the trend toward broader acceptance. The court might avoid constitutional questions on Proposition 8 and DOMA by focusing on 'standing,' or the legal eligibility of those arguing the case. If the court dismisses the Proposition 8 case, lower court rulings could allow same-sex marriages in California. Justice Sotomayor questioned the timing of the Proposition 8 case, suggesting that states should have more time to experiment and that society should have more time to find its direction. Dismissing the case on standing grounds could nullify previous rulings and potentially require a restart in lower courts, limiting the reach of gay marriage in California. A future statewide referendum could resolve the issue. Obama's support for gay marriage and refusal to defend DOMA could lead the court to dismiss the DOMA case on standing grounds, though many expect a ruling based on the law's merits. The court's decisions will face both approval and condemnation, but its authority is final. Justice Robert Jackson stated, 'We are not final because we are infallible, but we are infallible only because we are final.'
translated_content: Gli ultimi giorni di giugno della Corte Suprema, spesso chiamati 'stagione delle piene', comportano uno sforzo concentrato per completare il lavoro prima della pausa estiva. Questo mandato è particolarmente significativo, con sentenze attese su due questioni importanti che potrebbero avere un impatto profondo sulla vita e sui precedenti legali. Lunedì, la corte ha affrontato le ammissioni scolastiche basate sulla razza all'Università del Texas, ma ha rinviato il caso ai tribunali inferiori, evitando una decisione ampia sulla violazione dei diritti di pari protezione di alcuni candidati bianchi. Le questioni chiave in attesa di decisione includono:   -- Matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso: Appelli che mettono alla prova il diritto costituzionale delle coppie gay e lesbiche di sposarsi.   -- Diritto di voto: Il futuro del Voting Rights Act e la supervisione federale delle elezioni negli stati con una storia di discriminazione. Secondo Thomas Goldstein, un importante avvocato di Washington, le decisioni della corte influenzeranno tutti gli americani. Prevede che la corte potrebbe non sostenere pienamente le disposizioni esecutive del Voting Rights Act e potrebbe cercare una via di mezzo sul matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso, evitando una sentenza definitiva a favore o contro. Il calendario della corte per il rilascio di queste delicate sentenze non è fisso, ma mira a concludere il suo lavoro entro giovedì o all'inizio di luglio. I giudici hanno già votato sui casi pendenti dopo le discussioni orali. I singoli giudici stanno redigendo pareri, dissensi e concordanze in segreto. Il giudice Ruth Bader Ginsburg ha osservato la tradizione di discrezione della corte, affermando: 'Alla Corte Suprema, chi sa non parla. E chi parla, non sa'. La corte mira a finalizzare le bozze dei pareri entro il 1° giugno, con dissensi e concordanze dovuti entro il 15 giugno. I voti finali possono cambiare. I giudici e i loro assistenti legali stanno lavorando intensamente per finalizzare i pareri, garantendo l'accuratezza dei fatti e la validità legale. Le decisioni plasmeranno l'eredità dei giudici. Mentre i risultati possono essere contestati, il ragionamento costituzionale deve essere solido. Prevedere i risultati è una pratica comune a Washington, ma non sempre accurata. I casi sul matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso hanno attirato un'attenzione significativa, con gli attivisti che si sono radunati durante le discussioni di marzo. Le questioni chiave includono:   -- Benefici federali: Il Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) definisce il matrimonio a livello federale come tra un uomo e una donna, influenzando i benefici federali per le coppie dello stesso sesso. Edie Windsor ha dovuto affrontare significative imposte di successione dopo la morte del suo coniuge a causa del DOMA.   -- Referendum statali: La corte sta valutando se uno stato possa revocare i diritti al matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso dopo averli concessi, come è successo in California con la Proposition 8. La decisione della corte la porrà al centro dell'attenzione nazionale, simile al suo coinvolgimento nella sentenza sull'Affordable Care Act. Nove stati e il District of Columbia attualmente consentono il matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso. Delaware, Rhode Island e Minnesota hanno recentemente approvato leggi in tal senso. Circa 120.000 coppie dello stesso sesso legalmente sposate risiedono negli Stati Uniti. Esistono opinioni divergenti sulla questione se la corte debba emettere una sentenza ampia sulla parità di protezione. Alcuni suggeriscono che i funzionari eletti dovrebbero guidare la questione del matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso, notando l'approvazione degli elettori in diversi stati. La California è l'unico stato ad aver sia consentito che revocato il matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso. Goldstein ritiene improbabile che la corte imponga il riconoscimento del matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso a livello nazionale, preferendo passi incrementali. I giudici sono consapevoli dell'evoluzione delle norme sociali e potrebbero evitare di contraddire la tendenza verso una più ampia accettazione. La corte potrebbe evitare questioni costituzionali sulla Proposition 8 e sul DOMA concentrandosi sulla 'legittimazione attiva', ovvero sull'ammissibilità legale di coloro che sostengono il caso. Se la corte respingesse il caso della Proposition 8, le sentenze dei tribunali inferiori potrebbero consentire i matrimoni tra persone dello stesso sesso in California. Il giudice Sotomayor ha messo in dubbio i tempi del caso della Proposition 8, suggerendo che gli stati dovrebbero avere più tempo per sperimentare e che la società dovrebbe avere più tempo per trovare la sua direzione. Respingere il caso per motivi di legittimazione attiva potrebbe annullare le sentenze precedenti e potenzialmente richiedere un nuovo inizio nei tribunali inferiori, limitando la portata del matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso in California. Un futuro referendum statale potrebbe risolvere la questione. Il sostegno di Obama al matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso e il rifiuto di difendere il DOMA potrebbero portare la corte a respingere il caso DOMA per motivi di legittimazione attiva, anche se molti si aspettano una sentenza basata sui meriti della legge. Le decisioni della corte saranno oggetto sia di approvazione che di condanna, ma la sua autorità è definitiva. Il giudice Robert Jackson ha affermato: 'Non siamo definitivi perché siamo infallibili, ma siamo infallibili solo perché siamo definitivi.'

article_content: By Ryan Gorman Published: 13:10 EST, November 5, 2013 | Updated: 14:25 EST, November 5, 2013 Tesla’s Model S is becoming the ‘it’ car among the U.S. jet set. The Elon Musk-designed electric car is now the most-registered car in eight of the nation’s 25 wealthiest zip codes, beating out luxury car makers long associated with affluent lifestyles. Although the battery-powered roadster has surpassed all other cars in many neighborhoods, these are primarily located in California, according to Edmunds. Very popular: A row of Tesla Motors Model S electric sedans are shown near San Francisco. Atherton, CA (1st overall) - 15.4% Los Altos Hills, CA (2nd overall) - 11.9% Portola Valley, CA (9th overall) - 11.2% Los Altos, CA (14th overall) - 9.3% Montecito, CA (17th overall) - 3.4% Newport Coast, CA (18th overall) - 2.8% Monte Sereno, CA (22nd overall) - 6.5% Woodside, CA (23rd overall) - 5.7% The futuristic car enjoys significant double-digit market share in some California communities, according to a detailed breakdown on the site. More than 15% of all cars registered in Atherton, the country’s wealthiest zip code with median home prices well above $6 million, are Teslas. Los Altos Hills comes in second with 11.9% of registered cars bearing the Tesla name, followed by Portola Valley at 11.2%. Most California towns experiencing high Model S sales are located in and around Tesla’s Palo Alto headquarters, Edmunds noted. Visionary: Tesla Motors Inc. CEO Elon Musk's bet on the future is slowly paying off, as more people purchase his Model S roadster. The only non-California zip codes reflecting at least a 1% market share for Tesla are Hamptons hotspot Water Mill, at 1.5%, and Manhattan’s West Village with 1%. article_content: If you plan to travel to the Northeast for Thanksgiving, consider starting your journey early. A nor'easter is forecast to bring heavy rain or snow to the region late Tuesday, potentially causing travel disruptions on Wednesday, which is traditionally the busiest travel day of the year, according to CNN meteorologists. CNN senior meteorologist Dave Hennen stated, 'All of the major metro areas in the Northeast will be affected by either heavy rain or heavy snow, accompanied by strong winds.' He noted that it's currently too early to determine which metro areas will be most severely impacted, but airport delays are anticipated in New York City, Philadelphia, Boston, and Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. Hennen added, 'The I-95 corridor may serve as the boundary between heavy snow and heavy rain. Regardless, travel in the Northeast will be hazardous, particularly in the interior sections, due to heavy snow.' American Airlines is offering waived rebooking fees for holiday travelers flying through 18 airports in the Northeast. In a press release, the airline announced: 'Customers holding tickets for American Airlines, American Eagle, or US Airways/US Airways Express flights on November 26 to, from, or through (the 18 airports) can change their flights without incurring a penalty. The ticket-reissue charge will be waived for one ticket change, and travel can commence as early as November 25 or as late as November 27, in accordance with American's current travel waiver.' AAA projects that 46 million Americans will travel 50 miles or more from home during the Thanksgiving weekend, marking the highest number of travelers since 2007, according to a press release. On a positive note, AAA indicates that those traveling by car are likely to benefit from lower gas prices compared to recent years. The current national average gas price is $2.85 per gallon, which is 43 cents per gallon lower than the average price during Thanksgiving in 2013. CNN meteorologist Chad Myers mentioned that a European computer model predicts up to a foot of snow in Connecticut and Massachusetts, while an American computer model forecasts less snow. He explained, 'This is more likely to be a rain event than a snow event. It's not quite cold enough for a significant snowfall. Snow is expected in the Poconos, the Alleghenies, and Vermont, but along the I-95 corridor, expect a mix of rain and snow.'

article_content: Scientists have discovered that diesel pollution hinders honeybees' ability to find flowers by altering the chemical composition of floral scents. Honeybees rely on floral odors to locate flowers that provide the best sources of pollen and nectar. However, diesel fumes can impair their ability to locate and recognize these plants, which could affect pollination and, ultimately, global food security. British researchers analyzed eight chemicals present in the scent of oilseed rape flowers. They mixed these chemicals with both clean air, which had no effect on the scent, and air containing diesel fumes. When mixed with diesel fumes, the volume of six of the eight chemicals decreased, and two completely disappeared within one minute. This altered the chemical composition of the scent as it reacted with nitrogen oxides (NOx) found in exhaust fumes. The researchers, from the University of Southampton, trained honeybees to recognize a synthetic oilseed rape perfume by rewarding them with a sugar solution when exposed to the scent, teaching them to extend their proboscis upon smelling it. When exposed to a synthetic floral odor lacking the chemicals affected by nitrogen oxides, the proportion of honeybees able to recognize the scent significantly decreased, according to the study published in the journal Scientific Reports. The researchers reported that the number of bees recognizing the odor dropped from 100 percent to 30 percent when the nitrogen oxide-affected chemicals were removed from the scent. Dr. Tracey Newman, a neuroscientist at the University of Southampton, stated, 'Diesel exposure alters floral odors, causing a significant enough change in the chemistry to impact the honeybee's ability to recognize that odor.' Honeybees form large colonies and are vital to pollination and food security. A strong colony can contain about 60,000 bees. Honeybee decline is attributed to several factors: The Varroa mite weakens bees by feeding on the blood of larvae, pupae, and adults. Infested colonies may die within a few years. Honeybees are susceptible to diseases caused by bacteria, fungi, and viruses, some of which are linked to colony decline. Neglect by beekeepers in managing Varroa mites can lead to colony death. Pesticides, including neonicotinoid insecticides, are harmful to bees. 'It's not just about a bee getting confused because there's a new smell around; the odor itself is being chemically altered,' the scientists explained. The scientists focused on diesel due to its high levels of particulates (PMs), which are known to be harmful to human health. However, nitrogen oxides are also present in petrol fumes, suggesting that pollution from road transport, in general, could be affecting bees. Impairing the ability of forager bees to find flowers can damage the health of colonies and reduce crop pollination. Professor Guy Poppy, an ecologist at the University of Southampton, noted, 'Honeybee pollination can significantly increase crop yields and is vital to the world's economy – contributing £430 million a year to the UK alone.' Dr. Tracey Newman stated that 'Diesel exposure is not the root of the problem in honeybees, but it adds to the list of stresses they face, potentially harming their health.' Dr. Giles Budge of the Food and Environment Research Agency said the researchers have identified 'a fresh issue to add to the many problems facing our insect pollinators: the potential for fumes to degrade flower scent.' He also noted that further research is needed to see if this laboratory problem exists in the wider environment. Friends of the Earth Nature Campaigner Paul de Zylva said, 'Bees are highly sophisticated creatures facing many threats, including air pollution, and this research is yet more evidence that they are under attack from all sides.' The group has called on the government to develop a 'bee action plan' to address the threats facing these creatures.

article_content: The rapid evolution of slang makes it nearly impossible to stay current. Have you encountered phrases like 'Skibidi toilet' or 'the millennial pause'? Do you still use the laughing emoji to show you're laughing out loud? If so, Gen Alpha, those born after 2010, likely consider your slang outdated. A recent TikTok video, viewed over 3.3 million times, features Nicole Pellegrino, a millennial TikTok strategy director, being educated by her Gen Alpha sister, Simone, and her sister's friend about her antiquated slang. Many twenty-somethings watching the video felt suddenly old and irrelevant. 'Why didn't anyone tell me 'slay' is no longer cool?' one viewer lamented. At the beginning of the video, Pellegrino, in her early 30s, asks the girls, 'I can't say, like, 'That's a slay'?' ('Slay,' originating in Black and Latin queer culture, is often used online to praise someone's impressive accomplishment.) Simone covered her mouth in shock, and both girls strongly advised against using the term. 'It's incredibly uncool,' Simone said about 'slay'. Pellegrino then inquired about the word 'bet,' often used as a substitute for 'sounds good' or 'OK,' receiving a disapproving response. Next, she asked about using the laughing emoji, which elicited an astonished reaction. 'Do you really use the laughing emoji? Seriously?' Simone asked. 'When something is funny, you use the crying emoji because nobody actually uses the laughing emoji,' she clarified. Simone also suggested using the skull emoji when joking about something insulting. Be warned. After her sister used 'GYAT' in a sentence, Pellegrino looked stunned. 'What is a GYAT? Is it a yacht?' she questioned. The girls were equally surprised that Pellegrino didn't know the term. They explained it means someone has a nice butt ('Girl Your Ass Is Thick'). One girl offered an example: 'If you have a BBL or your butt shakes when you walk, you would yell GYAT at someone.' (However, many commenters disagreed with this definition, as online definitions vary. Some say it means 'girl you ate that,' while Urban Dictionary defines it as a polite version of 'goddamn.' It's also been used to mean 'get your act together,' according to Dexerto.) The TikTok hashtag for 'gyat' has 6.5 billion views, with popular posts featuring memes and butt-related jokes. The only slang Pellegrino used that seemed acceptable was 'okay period,' used to emphasize a point or show agreement. Thousands of comments on the video expressed feelings of aging as Gen Alpha creates new vocabulary and redefines existing terms. 'I'm 24 going on 100, apparently,' one commenter wrote. 'This made me feel ancient, and I'm only 25,' said another popular comment with 20,000 likes. Some viewers challenged the girls' analysis of outdated versus trendy slang. Many claimed that 'slay' is still popular or that the girls were using 'TikTok language.' The post sparked numerous responses in all caps. 'I FINALLY LEARNED WHAT GYAT MEANS! THANK YOU JESUS!' one person wrote. 'THEY ASSIGNED WORDS TO GYAT?!' another said. Others resigned themselves to being out of touch, sarcastically questioning the usefulness of such slang. 'Okay! You got us,' one person said. 'Now ask them how to spell 'restaurant.'' Insider has contacted Pellegrino for her input.

article_content: The BBC's new comedy, 'Citizen Khan', featuring a Muslim community leader, sparked debate upon its debut. Approximately 200 complaints were lodged with the BBC following the initial broadcast. Viewers suggested the program ridiculed Islam, perpetuated Asian stereotypes, and disrespected the Koran. The trailer is available for viewing. A controversial scene depicted Mr. Khan's daughter, heavily made-up, quickly donning a hijab and feigning reading from the Koran upon her father's entrance. Adil Ray, the British Muslim creator and star of the six-part BBC1 series, believes the show allows the Muslim community to find humor within itself. Some viewers expressed disappointment, citing disrespectful depictions, while others defended the show's comedic intent. The series explores the life of a Muslim community leader, navigating family matters such as a daughter's wedding plans. Critics argue it reinforces British Muslim stereotypes, unlike 'Goodness Gracious Me', despite sharing writers Anil Gupta and Richard Pinto. A BBC representative stated that the show had a successful launch with 3.6 million viewers and a 21.5% share, noting that new comedies often elicit varied reactions, and the characters are intended as comedic creations, not representative of the community. Ray clarified on BBC Breakfast that the program intends to enable the British Pakistani Muslim community to 'laugh at ourselves'.
